title: Distributed locks, leader election, ZooKeeper/etcd, fencing tokens
scopeHtml:
Scope: Lease locks, paused-holder problem, fencing tokens, Redis/Redlock, ZooKeeper and etcd recipes, leader election, DB locks.

Scope: Lease locks, paused-holder problem, fencing tokens, Redis/Redlock, ZooKeeper and etcd recipes, leader election, DB locks.

notes.title: Why distributed locks exist
notes.html:
A distributed lock lets only one process across many machines do a job at a time. Examples: only one worker runs the nightly billing job, only one node renews a shared cache, only one writer updates a file in object storage.

First ask whether you need a lock at all. Cheaper alternatives:

  • Database constraint or row lock: UPDATE ... WHERE status='NEW' or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
  • Idempotency: make doing the job twice harmless.
  • Single consumer per partition: Kafka gives one consumer per partition in a group.
  • Optimistic concurrency: version column, compare-and-set.

Two reasons to lock (Martin Kleppmann's framing):

  1. Efficiency: avoid doing duplicate work. If the lock fails occasionally, you just waste some CPU. A simple Redis lock is fine.
  2. Correctness: two holders corrupt data. Then you need a lock with fencing, built on consensus.

Worked example. 20 pods each run a cron at 02:00 to send daily emails to 1M users. Without a lock: 20x duplicate emails. With a lock (or a leader): one pod does the job in about 10 minutes. With idempotent INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING per (user, date), duplicates are harmless and you may need no lock.

Industry examples. Kubernetes controllers use a lease object in etcd for leader election; Spring Batch and Quartz use DB locks; Uber's Cadence/Temporal use consensus-backed storage to ensure one workflow owner.

Everyday analogy. One key to a shared meeting room: whoever holds the key can use it, everyone else waits.

Common interview traps.

  • Reaching for a distributed lock when a unique constraint would do.
  • Not saying whether the lock is for efficiency or correctness.

notes.title: Lease-based locks, TTLs and the paused-process problem
notes.html:
A lock must expire, or a crashed holder blocks everyone forever. So distributed locks are leases: a lock with a time limit (TTL).

Flow: acquire with TTL 30 s, do work, extend (heartbeat) every 10 s, release when done. If the holder dies, the lock vanishes after at most 30 s.

The nasty problem: the holder cannot know that its lease expired. A long GC pause, VM freeze, slow disk or network stall can stop it for longer than the TTL. When it wakes up it still believes it holds the lock and writes to the resource, while a second holder already took over.

t=0    A acquires lock (TTL 30s)
t=5    A starts a long GC pause (45 s)
t=30   lock expires
t=31   B acquires lock, writes to storage
t=50   A wakes up, still thinks it holds the lock, writes to storage  <-- CORRUPTION

The lock service cannot fix this; the resource must defend itself (fencing tokens, next section).

Real incident pattern. Intermittent duplicated or overwritten records only under load or during GC storms. Metric: GC pause duration p99 near or above the lease TTL; lock "lost" log lines appear after the damage.

Decision gravity. TTL choice: short means fast failover but more false expiries during pauses; long means slow recovery. Common: TTL 10 to 30 s, renew at one third of TTL. Reversible config, but the correctness model (fencing or not) is a one-way design decision.

Industry examples. Chubby (Google) popularised coarse-grained leases; DynamoDB lock client and Kubernetes Lease objects use TTL leases. Kubernetes defaults for leader election: lease duration 15 s, renew deadline 10 s, retry period 2 s (confirm in the client-go docs for your version).

Everyday analogy. A hotel keycard that stops working at noon: if you fell asleep in the room past noon, housekeeping enters; you still think the room is yours.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "I checked I hold the lock just before writing" is safe. The pause can happen after the check.
  • Using wall-clock time to decide lease validity (clock jumps). Use monotonic time with a safety margin.

notes.title: Fencing tokens
notes.html:
A fencing token is a number that increases every time the lock is granted. The protected resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any request carrying a lower one.

This solves the paused-holder problem: the stale holder's write carries an old token and is refused.

A acquires lock -> token 33
A pauses
lock expires; B acquires -> token 34
B writes with token 34   -> storage records max=34, OK
A wakes, writes token 33 -> storage: 33 < 34, REJECT

Requirements:

  • The lock service issues strictly increasing tokens (ZooKeeper zxid/node version, etcd revision, or a counter in a consensus store).
  • The resource must check tokens. That means the database, storage or downstream API has to participate (e.g. a column fence BIGINT with UPDATE ... WHERE fence <= :token). If the resource cannot, fencing is impossible and you need to use the resource's own atomic compare-and-set instead.
-- Storage-side fencing check, atomic
UPDATE jobs
SET payload = :p, fence = :token
WHERE id = :id AND fence <= :token;   -- 0 rows updated => stale holder, abort

Industry examples. HDFS NameNode HA fences the old active namenode (including storage-level fencing with shared edit logs). Kafka uses producer epochs and leader epochs as fencing tokens. Raft terms play the same role.

Decision gravity. Fencing is a design-level choice: adopt it when correctness matters. Alternative STONITH-style fencing powers off the node (heavy, used in HA clusters). Retrofitting token checks into a resource later is hard, so decide early.

Everyday analogy. Numbered tickets at a ticket window: the clerk only serves a ticket with a number at least as high as the last served; an old ticket is turned away.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the lock prevents two writers". With pauses it does not, without fencing.
  • Putting the token check in the client rather than the storage.
  • Using random UUIDs as tokens; they must be monotonic.

notes.title: Redis locks and Redlock
notes.html:
Simple Redis lock: SET lock:billing <random-id> NX PX 30000. NX means set only if absent; PX is the TTL in ms. Release with a Lua script that deletes only if the value still equals your random id (so you never delete someone else's lock).

# acquire
redis-cli SET lock:billing 7f3a-uuid NX PX 30000
# release (atomic compare-and-delete)
redis-cli EVAL "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 lock:billing 7f3a-uuid

Problems:

  • Single Redis master fails over asynchronously: the lock write may not have reached the replica, so a promoted replica lets a second client acquire. Two holders.
  • No built-in fencing token.
  • TTL pause problem as above.

Redlock (antirez's proposal) acquires the lock on a majority of N=5 independent Redis masters within a small time bound. Kleppmann's critique: it depends on bounded clocks and delays and gives no fencing token, so it is unsafe for correctness, though fine for efficiency. Antirez disputed parts of this. Interview-safe position: Redis locks are acceptable for efficiency; for correctness use a consensus-based system with fencing.

Worked example. Rate: a single Redis does about 100,000 SET ops/s, so lock throughput is rarely the limit. 1,000 pods contending for one lock every 30 s is trivial load.

Industry examples. Redisson (Java) and redis-py implement lock helpers; Shopify and many companies use Redis locks for de-duplication of jobs.

Decision gravity. Starting with a Redis lock is cheap and reversible, provided the protected action is idempotent. Moving to a consensus lock later is a modest change if you kept the lock behind an interface.

Everyday analogy. A sign on a door written in pencil: quick, but if the sign-keeper loses their notebook another person may write a second sign.

Common interview traps.

  • Releasing with a plain DEL (can delete another client's lock).
  • Using SETNX then EXPIRE as two commands (crash between them leaves a permanent lock). Use one atomic SET NX PX.
  • Calling Redlock "provably safe".

notes.title: ZooKeeper and etcd as coordination services
notes.html:
ZooKeeper and etcd are small, strongly consistent, replicated stores built on consensus (ZAB and Raft). They are designed for locks, leader election, configuration and service discovery, not for bulk data.

ZooKeeper primitives:

  • znodes in a tree; ephemeral znodes vanish when the client session ends (session timeout, say 10 s); sequential znodes get an increasing suffix; watches notify clients of changes.
  • Lock recipe: create ephemeral+sequential /lock/node-000000042. List children; if yours has the lowest number you hold the lock; otherwise watch only the node just before yours (avoids a thundering herd on release). The sequence number or zxid can act as a fencing token.

etcd primitives:

  • Key-value with a global revision (monotonic), leases with TTL (keys attached to a lease disappear when it expires), transactions (compare-and-swap), and watch streams.
  • Lock recipe: create key /lock/billing/<leaseID> with the lease, the holder with the lowest creation revision wins; the revision is the fencing token. The concurrency package in Go provides Mutex and Election.

Typical limits. etcd values are meant to be small (default request limit about 1.5 MiB, DB quota default 2 GB; confirm per version). ZooKeeper znode data limit is about 1 MB by default and it keeps all data in memory. A 3 or 5 node ensemble handles roughly thousands to tens of thousands of writes/s; reads scale with followers.

Industry examples. Kubernetes stores all state in etcd; Kafka (older versions) used ZooKeeper for controller election and metadata (now KRaft); HBase, Hadoop HA and Solr use ZooKeeper; Consul offers sessions and KV locks on Raft.

Decision gravity. Choosing a managed coordination service is a deliberate dependency: operationally heavy but battle-tested. Alternative: lease row in your existing Postgres (simple, one fewer system, but not designed for high churn). Moving between them is moderately reversible if hidden behind a leader-election interface.

Everyday analogy. A notary office: small, slow, extremely careful records that everyone trusts, as opposed to a fast but forgetful notice board.

Common interview traps.

  • Using ZooKeeper/etcd as a general database or queue.
  • Forgetting session timeout vs lease TTL: a client that stalls loses ephemeral nodes.
  • Having every waiter watch the same node (thundering herd).

notes.title: Leader election
notes.html:
Leader election picks one node among many to act as the coordinator or sole writer, and picks a new one if it fails. It is the same problem as a distributed lock held for a long time.

Approaches:

  1. Built into the data system: Raft/Paxos groups (etcd, Kafka KRaft, CockroachDB ranges) elect leaders internally.
  2. Lock-based: all candidates try to create the same lease key; the winner is leader and keeps renewing. If it stops renewing, others compete again (Kubernetes controller manager, scheduler).
  3. Database row: UPDATE leader SET owner=:me, expires=now()+30s WHERE expires < now() OR owner=:me. Simple, with the caveats of clocks and fencing.
  4. Bully / ring algorithms: textbook, rarely used in production.
# Kubernetes leader election flags for controllers (typical values)
leaderElection:
  leaderElect: true
  leaseDuration: 15s
  renewDeadline: 10s
  retryPeriod: 2s

Failover time is about the lease duration plus retry period: here 15 to 17 s. Shorter means faster failover but more flapping on a GC pause or API server slowness.

Worked example. 3 replicas of a scheduler pod, leader dies at t=0. Lease (15 s) expires at t=15 s, standby tries at its next retry (within 2 s) and wins by t=17 s. Scheduling stalls for about 17 s but no duplicate scheduling occurs.

What the old leader must do. Stop acting the moment it fails to renew (step down quickly: renewDeadline < leaseDuration) and also be protected by fencing at the resource.

Industry examples. Kafka partition leaders (ISR-based, with leader epochs), HDFS active/standby namenodes with ZKFC, Elasticsearch master election, Kubernetes components via Lease objects.

Decision gravity. Single leader is simple and high throughput but has failover pauses and a ceiling at one node's capacity. Alternatives: partition work so each partition has its own leader (sharding), or leaderless designs with conflict resolution. Moving between them is a major architecture change.

Everyday analogy. A relay baton: whoever holds it is in charge, and if the runner collapses, the team picks the next runner after a short pause.

Common interview traps.

  • Not handling the old leader still running (zombie leader).
  • Having failover time shorter than the longest realistic GC or network pause.
  • Believing a leader election makes the leader's side effects safe without fencing.

notes.title: Database-based locks and advisory locks
notes.html:
Sometimes the lock service you already have, a relational DB, is the right tool. Options in Postgres:

  • Row lock: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a row; released at commit/rollback. A crashed connection releases automatically.
  • Advisory locks: pg_advisory_lock(key) (session scoped) or pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) (transaction scoped); locks are on application-chosen numbers, not rows. pg_try_advisory_lock does not block.
  • Queue pattern: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10 lets many workers pull different jobs safely.
-- Only one worker runs the job; others skip immediately
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42);   -- returns true for one session only
-- ... do work ...
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42);

-- Job queue pattern
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'NEW'
ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Why it works well: the lock is tied to the connection or transaction; if the process dies the DB frees it, with no TTL guessing. Caveats: ties up a connection per lock; works only if everyone talks to the same primary (not across replicas or regions); session-level advisory locks leak through connection poolers like PgBouncer in transaction mode (use transaction-level locks there).

Worked example. 50 workers, a jobs table. SKIP LOCKED lets each take a 10-row batch with no blocking; throughput of several thousand jobs/s on one Postgres is realistic.

Industry examples. Que, GoodJob, River and Oban (queue libraries) use Postgres SKIP LOCKED/advisory locks; Rails' with_advisory_lock gems; Flyway/Liquibase use a lock to serialise migrations.

Decision gravity. Easy, reversible, but it ties availability of the lock to your primary database and adds load there. Good until the lock contention itself becomes a hot spot.

Everyday analogy. A shared whiteboard marker held by whoever is at the board; if they walk out of the building, security takes it back automatically.

Common interview traps.

  • Session advisory locks behind a transaction-mode pooler.
  • Holding a row lock across a slow external call (blocks others, long transactions bloat the DB).

notes.title: Common failure scenarios and a decision guide
notes.html:
Scenarios to reason through in an interview:

Failure What happens Defence
Holder crashes Lease expires, others proceed TTL / session / DB frees lock
Holder paused (GC, VM) Two believe they hold the lock Fencing token checked by resource
Network partition Holder cannot renew Holder steps down at renewDeadline
Lock service loses quorum No one can acquire Fail closed (stop the job) or degrade deliberately
Clock jump Lease length misjudged Monotonic clocks, safety margin
Lock service failover (Redis) Lock lost Use consensus store when correctness matters

Heuristics:

  • Idempotency beats locks. If the job can be repeated safely, a lock only saves cost.
  • Keep critical sections short and never hold a lock over a remote call you cannot bound.
  • Fail closed if you cannot confirm the lock: stop and retry rather than proceed.
  • Add a timeout to acquiring too, with jitter on retries.

Everyday analogy. Booking the only meeting room: the booking system is useful, but you also lock the door from inside so a late-arriving group cannot walk in on stale information.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing the happy path only. The interviewer asks "what if the holder freezes for 60 seconds?"
  • Choosing a lock service with no discussion of its failure mode.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• First try to avoid locks: unique constraints, idempotency, single consumer per partition, optimistic CAS.
  • Distributed locks are leases with TTLs; a paused holder cannot know it lost the lease.
  • Fencing tokens (monotonic numbers checked by the resource) make locks safe for correctness; Raft terms, Kafka epochs and etcd revisions are the same idea.
  • Redis SET NX PX plus a safe unlock script is fine for efficiency; Redlock is debated and gives no fencing.
  • ZooKeeper (ephemeral+sequential znodes, watch predecessor) and etcd (leases, revisions, txn) are consensus-backed coordination services; keep data small.
  • Leader election = long-held lock; failover time is about lease duration plus retry period; the old leader must step down and be fenced.
  • Postgres advisory locks and SKIP LOCKED are excellent for simple cases; beware poolers and long transactions.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use a distributed lock, and what would you try first instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-use of locks is a classic smell; the strong answer starts by avoiding them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A distributed lock makes sure only one process across many machines does a job at a time. First I ask whether I need one: a unique constraint or conditional update, an idempotent operation, a single consumer per partition, or optimistic concurrency often do the job. Then I ask why I lock: for efficiency (avoid duplicate work; a failure only wastes CPU, so a simple Redis lock is fine) or for correctness (two holders corrupt data; then I need a consensus-backed lock with fencing).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Alternatives: UPDATE ... WHERE status='NEW', SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, Kafka consumer groups, version column with compare-and-set.
  • Efficiency vs correctness (Kleppmann's framing) decides the tool and how much to invest.
  • Example: 20 pods run a 02:00 cron to email 1M users. Without a lock: 20x duplicates. With idempotent per-(user,date) inserts you may need no lock at all.
Worker1 -> lock service -> granted
Worker2 -> lock service -> denied, wait/skip
Worker3 -> lock service -> denied, wait/skip

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reaching for a lock when a unique constraint is enough.
  • Not stating whether it is for efficiency or correctness.
  • Forgetting the lock must expire if the holder dies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the job is not idempotent? -> Make it so (idempotency key), or use a lock with fencing.
  2. Why do locks expire? -> A crashed holder must not block everyone forever; hence leases.
  3. Where do Kubernetes controllers get a lock? -> A Lease object in etcd, used for leader election.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior: "use Redis SETNX". Senior: tries avoiding the lock, classifies efficiency vs correctness, and names the failure modes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Duplicate emails and double charges from "cron on N pods" without any coordination.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement a safe single-instance Redis lock, and where does it still fail?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests atomicity awareness and honesty about limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Acquire with one atomic command, SET lock:billing <random-id> NX PX 30000: NX sets only if absent, PX is the TTL. Release with a Lua script that deletes the key only if its value still equals my random id, so I never delete someone else's lock. It still fails when Redis fails over asynchronously (the lock write may not have reached the replica), when the holder pauses past the TTL, and because there is no fencing token. So it is fine for efficiency, not for correctness.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
# acquire (atomic)
redis-cli SET lock:billing 7f3a-uuid NX PX 30000
# release: compare-and-delete in one atomic script
redis-cli EVAL "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 lock:billing 7f3a-uuid
  • Random value identifies the owner. Plain DEL could remove a lock that expired and was taken by another client.
  • SETNX then EXPIRE as two commands: a crash between them leaves a lock that never expires.
  • Renew (extend) the TTL only if you still own it, again via script.
  • Redlock (acquire on a majority of 5 independent masters) is debated; it assumes bounded clocks and pauses and provides no fencing token.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Plain DEL for release.
  • Two-step SETNX/EXPIRE.
  • Calling Redlock "provably safe".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What throughput limit? -> A single Redis does about 100,000 simple ops/s, so lock rate is rarely the limit.
  2. How do I make the action safe anyway? -> Make it idempotent, or add a version check on the resource.
  3. What does WAIT do? -> Blocks until N replicas ack, reducing but not eliminating loss on failover (verify semantics).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior shows SETNX. Senior shows the atomic release, explains failover and pause failures and says when not to use it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Failover during a Redis maintenance gave two holders of a "singleton" job (see Q033).

questions.contextHtml: Your service runs 20 pods. At 02:00 a cron in every pod sends a "daily digest" email to 1M users; the job takes about 10 minutes when run by one pod. Today users get up to 20 emails. A teammate proposes a Redis lock with a 15-minute TTL. You are told only: "make sure exactly one email per user per day."
questions.promptHtml: How do you approach this? Evaluate the lock and propose alternatives.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the Redis lock." If the pod holding it dies at minute 9, a new holder restarts and users get duplicates anyway; and the TTL expiry before completion yields two runners.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is "exactly one" strict or best effort? Is the email provider idempotent (does it accept a dedupe key)? What if the job takes longer than 15 min? What happens on a crash mid-run?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run the cron on one designated pod via a Kubernetes CronJob (one run per schedule, concurrencyPolicy: Forbid) instead of in-app cron on 20 pods.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the lock only prevents concurrent runs, not repeated runs after a crash; (b) per-user idempotency is the true requirement; (c) a queue with one consumer per partition handles resume.
  4. How I'd verify each: Kill the job mid-run in staging and count duplicate sends.
  5. Root cause: The real requirement is per-user dedupe, which a job-level lock does not provide.
  6. Fix: Insert (user_id, digest_date) with a unique constraint before sending (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; send only if a row was inserted, mark sent after provider ack), and pass the same key to the provider if supported. Then parallelize safely: 20 pods can each take disjoint batches with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, finishing in about 30 seconds instead of 10 minutes, with no distributed lock.
  7. Prevention: Metric of duplicates per run (count of conflicts), alert if sent count != eligible count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Exactly-once with an external email provider is not truly possible; the strongest I can claim is at-most-once or at-least-once with dedupe. I would not rely on a TTL guess for correctness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Crash between send and DB mark? -> Either a rare duplicate (mark before send risks a missed email) or a provider idempotency key to bridge it.
  • Why not a lock then? -> It can still be a cheap optimization to avoid 20 pods scanning the same rows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "singleton cron" lock expired mid-run during a slow DB day, a second pod started, and both ran; per-row uniqueness made the second run harmless.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Redis lock only.
  • Hire: idempotent unique constraint plus batch claiming.
  • Strong hire: addresses exactly-once limits with external systems, crash windows and observability.

questions.contextHtml:
Operations notice that once a month the nightly billing job never runs again until someone deletes the lock key by hand, and twice the job ran concurrently on two hosts. The lock helper does this sequence (shown as redis-cli commands):

# acquire
redis-cli SETNX lock:billing 1
redis-cli EXPIRE lock:billing 30
# ... run job that usually takes 20 s but sometimes 70 s ...
# release
redis-cli DEL lock:billing

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a longer TTL." That fixes one symptom and creates slow recovery.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the process crash rate between the two commands? Does the job extend the lease? Does the job write to a resource that can validate a fence?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a TTL on the existing key and delete the stuck one.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SETNX and EXPIRE are separate: a crash between them leaves a never-expiring lock (the monthly stuck case); (b) job runs 70 s with TTL 30 s, so the lock expires while the first runner is still working and a second host acquires (the concurrent runs); (c) DEL at release can delete the second host's lock; (d) the value is the constant 1, so there is no ownership.
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli TTL lock:billing returning -1 means no expiry; log acquire/release with timestamps and holder id; reproduce with kill -9 between the commands.
  5. Root cause: Non-atomic acquire, no ownership, no renewal.
  6. Fix: SET lock:billing <uuid> NX PX 30000; heartbeat every 10 s extending only if value matches (Lua); release with compare-and-delete Lua; make the billing writes idempotent, and for correctness use fencing at the DB.
  7. Prevention: Use a vetted library (Redisson for Java, a maintained client helper elsewhere; verify features) instead of hand-written code; integration test with kill -9 and slow jobs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just bump TTL to 10 minutes: a crash then blocks billing for 10 minutes. Renewal threads themselves can stall during GC, so renewal does not replace fencing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Renewal thread freezes with the app? -> Lease can still expire; the resource must reject the stale holder (fencing).
  • Does Lua make it safe? -> It makes release atomic on one Redis; it does not fix failover or pauses.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A permanent-lock bug sat in a helper for a year because the crash window was microseconds; it appeared only when a node was OOM-killed at exactly the wrong moment.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer TTL.
  • Hire: atomic SET NX PX, owner token, safe release.
  • Strong hire: adds renewal pitfalls, idempotency, fencing and crash testing.

questions.contextHtml:
A JVM service uses a lease lock (TTL 30 s, renewed every 10 s) around updating a customer's ledger file in object storage. During a nightly spike, duplicated and overwritten entries appear for about 15 customers. Log excerpt:

02:14:07.100 acquired lock cust-881 ttl=30s
02:14:09.800 [gc] pause 41.2 s (G1 Full GC)
02:14:38.000 (other pod) acquired lock cust-881
02:14:40.400 (other pod) wrote ledger cust-881 version=412
02:14:51.100 writing ledger cust-881 version=412

Heap is 28 GB on a 32 GB container; GC pause p99 is about 30 s at night. Lock service dashboards show no errors.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Tune GC and extend the TTL." Reduces frequency but the problem class remains.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the storage do conditional writes? Is each ledger update idempotent? How many holders per customer should exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce heap pressure and add a safety check; reconcile the 15 customers from the event log.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pause longer than TTL: lock expired at 02:14:37 while pod A was frozen; pod B took it and wrote; A woke and wrote; (b) clock problems (red herring: timestamps are monotonic enough here); (c) lock service bug (dashboards clean).
  4. How I'd verify each: GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) vs lock events; compare lease timestamps; check the other pod's acquire time.
  5. Root cause: The holder cannot know its lease expired during a stop-the-world pause; a check "do I still hold the lock?" right before writing does not help because the pause can occur after the check.
  6. Fix: Fencing: lock service returns a monotonic token; the storage layer rejects writes with a lower token than seen (UPDATE ledger SET ... , fence=:t WHERE id=:id AND fence <= :t). Where storage cannot check, use its conditional write (ETag/version) as the check. Then reduce GC pauses as a secondary fix (heap size, collector choice, containerized memory).
  7. Prevention: Alert when pause duration > TTL/3; chaos test with SIGSTOP for 60 s; code review rule: every lock-protected write carries a fence.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: TTL 120 s slows failover to two minutes and still loses to a 3-minute pause. I would not trust the lock service as the sole barrier.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if storage ignores tokens? -> Wrap writes in a small service that does the check atomically, or use optimistic versioning.
  • Is renewing more often helpful? -> Only if the renewal thread is not itself paused; a full GC stops all threads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first fix was a larger TTL; the next quarter a VM live-migration stall of 90 s produced the same corruption.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes TTL or GC only.
  • Hire: identifies the pause and proposes fencing.
  • Strong hire: includes timeline analysis, storage-side check, chaos test, and secondary GC work.

questions.promptHtml: What is a fencing token, who generates it, who checks it, and why can't the lock service alone make a lock safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The litmus test for understanding the paused-holder problem and the Kleppmann/Redlock debate.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A fencing token is a number that increases every time the lock is granted. The lock service issues it; the protected resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any request with a lower one. A paused holder wakes up believing it holds the lock, but its token is old, so the resource refuses the write. The lock service alone cannot do this because it has no control over what the stale holder does after the lease expired; the check must live at the resource.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A acquires lock -> token 33
A pauses; lease expires; B acquires -> token 34
B writes (34): storage max=34 OK
A wakes, writes (33): 33 < 34 -> REJECT
UPDATE jobs SET payload = :p, fence = :token
WHERE id = :id AND fence <= :token;   -- 0 rows => stale holder, abort
  • Sources of monotonic tokens: ZooKeeper zxid or znode version, etcd revision, a counter in a consensus store, Raft term, Kafka producer/leader epoch.
  • UUIDs are not tokens: they are not ordered.
  • If the resource cannot check, use its native compare-and-set (version, ETag) or STONITH-style fencing (power off or cut off the node).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "The lock prevents two writers" (false under pauses).
  • Putting the check in the client instead of the storage.
  • Random IDs as tokens.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Redis give tokens? -> Not by itself; you could keep a counter, but failover can lose it.
  2. How is it like Raft terms? -> Both are epochs: messages from older epochs are rejected.
  3. What if two resources are updated? -> Each must check, or one resource is the system of record.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior: "a number in the lock". Senior: where the check lives, token sources, and what to do when the resource cannot cooperate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: HDFS NameNode HA and Kafka (epochs) rely on this to stop zombie leaders from writing.

questions.contextHtml: You need a lock for three different uses in one platform: (1) a nightly report generator (duplicate runs just waste 5 minutes of CPU), (2) ensuring one worker at a time rebuilds a search index (a double rebuild corrupts the index unless fenced), (3) a job queue where 50 workers each claim 10 jobs at a time from a Postgres jobs table at about 2,000 jobs/s. Available: Redis (existing), etcd (used by Kubernetes, not by your app), Postgres (primary store).
questions.promptHtml: Pick a mechanism for each use and justify, including failure behaviour.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One tool for all three, e.g. "use Redis everywhere" or "etcd everywhere".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the index store do conditional writes? Is the report job idempotent? Can Postgres handle the extra queue load?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Use 1 is efficiency, use 2 is correctness, use 3 is a queue pattern, not a lock at all.
  4. How I'd verify each: Chaos tests: kill -9 holder, SIGSTOP for 60 s, Redis failover, etcd member loss.
  5. Root cause of the distinction: failure cost differs: duplicates waste CPU vs corrupt data vs nothing if rows are claimed atomically.
  6. Fix / choice: (1) Redis SET NX PX with safe release; accept rare duplicates. (2) etcd lease lock (or ZooKeeper) with the revision as fencing token, and the index writer rejects stale tokens; if the index store cannot check, use its version/ETag compare-and-set. (3) Postgres SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10; the claim is a transaction, a crashed worker's rows return automatically; several thousand jobs/s on one Postgres is realistic.
  7. Prevention: Hide each behind an interface (LockService) so you can swap; define a failure policy: fail closed.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: etcd adds an operational dependency; if the platform cannot run it, I would use Postgres advisory locks for (2) with a fence column on the same DB. I would not use Redlock for (2).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Postgres primary fails over? -> Advisory/row locks vanish with the connection; new holder proceeds; fence column protects the old writer.
  • Redis unavailable for (1)? -> Fail open or closed by explicit policy; here skipping the report for one night is acceptable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A platform standardized on "the lock service" and used it for a hot queue; it became the busiest consumer of its consensus cluster.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single tool.
  • Hire: efficiency vs correctness vs queue.
  • Strong hire: fencing, failure policy, abstraction, chaos tests.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the ZooKeeper distributed lock recipe. Why does each waiter watch only its predecessor, and how does etcd do the equivalent?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of herd effects and of coordination primitives, not just "use ZooKeeper".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each client creates an ephemeral, sequential znode under /lock, such as /lock/node-0000042. It lists the children; if its node has the lowest sequence number it holds the lock, otherwise it sets a watch on the node just before its own and waits. Watching only the predecessor means a release wakes exactly one waiter instead of all (no thundering herd). The ephemeral node disappears when the session dies, so a crash frees the lock. etcd does this with leases and key creation revisions: lowest revision wins, attached to a lease.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Ephemeral = tied to client session (session timeout, say 10 s); sequential = server assigns increasing suffix; watch = one-time notification.
  • Chain: A holds (node-1), B watches node-1, C watches node-2. If B dies, its node vanishes, C's watch fires, and C re-checks the list.
  • The sequence number or zxid can be the fencing token.
  • etcd: key /lock/billing/<leaseID> attached to a lease with TTL; waiters watch the key with the next-lower revision; revision is the fencing token; Go's concurrency package provides Mutex and Election.
  • A client that stalls beyond its session timeout loses ephemeral nodes (like a lease expiring); again the resource must fence.
/lock/node-001 (A, holds)  <- B watches
/lock/node-002 (B)         <- C watches
/lock/node-003 (C)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Everyone watching the same node (herd).
  • Using ZooKeeper/etcd as a general database or queue (small values only; about 1 MB znode data, etcd about 1.5 MiB requests; verify for version).
  • Forgetting the session-expiry semantics.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens when the waiter's predecessor is not the holder but dies? -> Its watch fires; it re-lists children and checks whether it is now lowest.
  2. How are ephemeral nodes and GC pauses related? -> A long pause can expire the session; the paused client still thinks it holds the lock.
  3. ZooKeeper vs etcd? -> Different protocols (ZAB vs Raft) and APIs; both consensus-backed, so equal safety class; choose by ecosystem.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior: "ephemeral nodes". Senior: predecessor watch, sessions vs leases, token source, and pause caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A lock recipe where all clients watched /lock caused a stampede of thousands of getChildren calls on each release.

questions.contextHtml: A payouts job takes a Redis lock (SET payout:lock <id> NX PX 60000) so only one worker issues settlement transfers. During a Redis maintenance failover (primary to replica with async replication), two workers ran the payout concurrently for about 40 seconds. 37 merchants were paid twice, total about 52,000 in duplicate payouts. Redis logs show the old primary accepted SET 80 ms before it was demoted; the new primary had no such key. App logs: both workers logged lock acquired.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, how you contain the money impact now, and what the long-term design is.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Redlock." The notes and the debate show Redlock still depends on timing and has no fencing token.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do payouts carry an idempotency key to the bank/PSP? Can we freeze payouts now? How did the second worker not see the first worker's run?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the payout job, reconcile the 37 duplicates against the PSP, start recovery/clawback with finance and the provider.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) async replication lost the lock key on failover (confirmed by timing); (b) worker paused beyond TTL (60 s) (red herring: only 40 s overlap); (c) client retry created a second lock.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare Redis replication offset/INFO replication at failover; app logs; payout ledger rows per (merchant, period).
  5. Root cause: Redis replication is asynchronous; the lock write was acknowledged on the old primary but absent after promotion, so the lock was effectively granted twice.
  6. Fix: Correctness lives in the data: payout idempotency key (merchant, period) with a unique constraint and pass it to the PSP; lock moves to a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) with a fencing token for the ledger, or a DB row lock/advisory lock in the same database as the ledger. Redis lock remains only as an optimization.
  7. Prevention: Failover game days with "two holders" assertions; reconciliation job comparing payouts to expected; review rule: no money moves behind a Redis lock alone.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: WAIT 1 ... reduces the window but cannot guarantee; Redlock across 5 masters is operationally heavy and still not fenced. Idempotency is the cheaper, stronger fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PSP does not support idempotency keys? -> Keep our own outbox with state machine (PENDING, SENT, CONFIRMED) and reconcile.
  • Why not just retry less? -> The problem is concurrent holders, not retries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scheduled Redis upgrade turned into a finance incident because the lock was treated as a correctness mechanism; the post-mortem renamed it "best-effort dedupe" in the code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Redlock as the answer.
  • Hire: idempotency plus consensus-backed lock.
  • Strong hire: money-impact containment, reconciliation, game days, precise explanation of async failover loss.

questions.contextHtml: A scheduler runs 3 replicas with Kubernetes-style leader election (leaseDuration: 15s, renewDeadline: 10s, retryPeriod: 2s). Failover after a leader crash takes about 17 s of scheduling stall. Product now wants failover under 3 s. Observed on this service: JVM full-GC pauses up to 4 s at p99 on a busy day; API server (lease store) p99 latency 800 ms with occasional 3 s spikes.
questions.promptHtml: Can you hit 3 s by changing the settings? Reason it through and give the options.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set leaseDuration 3s, renewDeadline 2s." It flaps constantly given 4 s GC pauses.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does a stalled scheduler cost (jobs delayed or user impact)? Is it acceptable to briefly have no leader? Can work be partitioned?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; 17 s is a performance goal, not an outage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: failover ~ leaseDuration + retryPeriod (15 + 2); a lease shorter than the worst pause or store latency produces false expiries and leader churn, each churn re-electing and possibly double acting.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure p99.9 GC pause and lease-renew latency; replay settings in staging with injected pauses; count leader transitions per hour.
  5. Root cause of the tension: The old leader cannot distinguish "dead" from "slow"; the lease must outlast the longest tolerated pause plus store latency.
  6. Fix / options: (a) keep 15 s (or lower to about 8 to 10 s only after reducing GC pauses to under 1 s); (b) warm standby: followers pre-load state so takeover work is instant and only the lease wait remains; (c) partition the scheduler (e.g. 16 shards, each its own lease) so a failover stalls only 1/16 of work; (d) reduce pauses (heap sizing, collector tuning).
  7. Prevention: Metrics for leader transitions, lease renew latency; fence leader-only writes with a token so a late old leader is harmless.
# example tuned config only AFTER pauses are fixed (renewDeadline < leaseDuration)
leaderElection:
  leaderElect: true
  leaseDuration: 8s
  renewDeadline: 6s
  retryPeriod: 1s
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set a 3 s lease while p99 pause is 4 s: constant flapping is worse than a 17 s stall. Sub-second failover generally needs a different design (active-active with partitioned work).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leader detects its own failed renewal? -> It must stop acting at renewDeadline, before the lease expires for others.
  • Lease store slow? -> Failover also slows; consider a closer or dedicated store.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Lowering the lease to 5 s "for faster failover" caused nightly leader churn during GC; moving to sharded leases removed the need for fast failover at all.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shrinks timeouts.
  • Hire: relates the lease to pauses and latency.
  • Strong hire: options (warm standby, sharded leases), fencing, and tied to cost of a stall.

questions.contextHtml: A singleton job takes SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42) at start and pg_advisory_unlock(42) at end, behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. After a deploy, the job runs once and then never again; try_lock returns false everywhere. Postgres warnings in logs: WARNING: you don't own a lock of type ExclusiveLock. SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype='advisory' shows objid=42 held by backend pid 9114 which is idle, and no application owns it. Connection count looks normal.
questions.promptHtml: Explain exactly why this happened and fix it, both now and permanently.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart Postgres." It would work once and recur.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which pool mode was used before the deploy? Did the job run in a transaction? How many replicas run the job?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Terminate backend 9114 (SELECT pg_terminate_backend(9114)) to release the session-level lock; verify with pg_locks.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) session-level lock acquired on one server connection, unlock executed on a different pooled connection after the pool rotated; (b) leaked lock from a crashed client (the lock would auto-release on disconnect, so less likely here); (c) a second app instance holding it (checked: idle backend).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_locks joined to pg_stat_activity (pid, state, query_start); PgBouncer SHOW POOLS/SHOW SERVERS.
  5. Root cause: In transaction pooling, each transaction may use a different server connection. Session advisory locks belong to a server connection, not to your logical client; the lock stays on pid 9114, which is returned to the pool, and unlock runs on another backend where you don't own it.
  6. Fix: Use transaction-scoped locks (pg_advisory_xact_lock/pg_try_advisory_xact_lock) inside one transaction that spans the critical section, or give the job a direct (session-mode) connection that bypasses PgBouncer.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule against pg_advisory_lock in pooled apps; integration tests run through the same pooler as production.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A long transaction holding a lock bloats the DB (vacuum, snapshots) and ties up a connection; for long jobs prefer a lease row with heartbeat and a fence. I would not disable pooling globally.
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(42) AS got;   -- released at COMMIT/ROLLBACK
-- if got: run the critical section in this same transaction
COMMIT;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lock must outlive one transaction? -> Use a lease table row with expires_at plus fencing, not an advisory lock.
  • Works across replicas/regions? -> No; locks are only on the primary that everyone connects to.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Enabling PgBouncer transaction mode as a "free scalability win" quietly broke every singleton job that relied on session locks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts DB.
  • Hire: identifies session vs pooled connection and uses xact locks.
  • Strong hire: gives release procedure, limits (long transactions), lease-row alternative, CI test.

questions.contextHtml: A compaction service rewrites a table-manifest file in object storage under a leader lease (etcd, 20 s TTL). In an incident, a leader paused for 70 s (VM live migration), woke up and overwrote the manifest written by the new leader; 6 hours of compaction results were lost and queries returned stale file lists. The lock service logs are clean: the old leader's lease had expired and a new leader (revision 5,210) was elected. The object store accepts plain PUTs; nobody reads tokens.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident analysis and design the fix when the storage cannot check fencing tokens natively.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more checks in the leader before writing." Those checks race with pauses.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the object store support conditional writes (put-if-absent, compare-on-ETag; verify current support and semantics for your provider)? Are there other systems that could hold the manifest pointer (a database row)? Who reads the manifest?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore the manifest from versioned history (enable bucket versioning), rerun compaction; pause the compaction leader during recovery.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) paused holder wrote after takeover (confirmed by timeline); (b) the lock service misbehaved (no, lease expired legitimately); (c) clock error (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare etcd lease expiry/revision history with the storage object version history and the VM migration event.
  5. Root cause: The lock was treated as safe for correctness but the resource never validated the epoch; paused holders can act after expiry.
  6. Fix: Make the manifest update a conditional write: use version-numbered manifests manifest-000412.json written with put-if-absent (only one writer can create a given version; the loser fails), plus a pointer updated by compare-and-swap in a small consensus-backed or SQL store using the fence (UPDATE pointer SET v=:v, fence=:t WHERE fence <= :t). Alternative: route writes through a thin service that enforces the token.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test SIGSTOP for 2x TTL; checklist "every lock-protected side effect is fenced"; bucket versioning and object lock for recovery.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not extend the TTL to 5 minutes; it only moves the window. Version-numbered manifests add garbage collection of old versions and slightly more read logic; a pointer service adds a dependency but is the simplest correct choice.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Object store has no conditional write at all? -> Use a database as the commit point and treat storage objects as immutable, unreferenced until committed.
  • Two compaction leaders by design (shards)? -> Fence per shard with a per-shard token.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "single writer" guarantee backed only by a lease worked for two years until a hypervisor migration stalled a pod for over a minute; the fix turned out to be a one-line conditional update.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer lease or pre-write checks.
  • Hire: fencing via storage-side compare-and-set.
  • Strong hire: handles storage limits (immutable versions plus pointer), recovery steps, chaos testing, blameless framing.
